frames.narration: 1,000 queries arrive, each asking for the sum of half of a 1,000-element array. Recomputing adds up 500 elements per query: 500,000 steps, and no extra memory.
A prefix-sum table stores running totals: 1,001 cells, built in 1,000 steps. Each query is then one subtraction, so 1,000 queries cost 2,000 steps in all. Memory was spent to save time.
The build cost has to be repaid. Each query saves 499 steps, so the 1,000-step build is repaid from the third query on. With just 2 queries, recomputing (1,000 steps) beats the table (1,002).

Why not store every range? A full n x n table also answers in one step, but it needs 1,000,000 cells and 1,000,000 build steps, and it only beats recomputing from 2,005 queries. It never beats the prefix table.
Now scale up. At n = 100,000 the full table needs 10 billion cells, about 80 GB at 8 bytes each. A fast algorithm that does not fit in memory is not fast. The memory budget is the second constraint.
The prefix table at n = 100,000 needs 100,001 cells, well within budget, and 101,000 steps for 1,000 queries against 50,000,000 for recomputing.

The other direction exists too: when data does not fit, recompute, stream or sketch (a Bloom filter says 'definitely not present' or 'probably present' in about 10 bits per item at a 1% false-positive rate) and pay in time or accuracy instead.

Last trap: a cache is a space-for-time trade with no ceiling unless you add one. With no eviction it grows with every new key (41,834 entries in the sample); a cap keeps memory bounded and gives up some hits.
